Every year, agencies across the United Nations use data to track major global challenges, like eradicating extreme poverty, lowering maternal mortality, halting epidemics and more.

These agencies work with some of the most valuable and trustworthy data in the world. But the statistics needed to solve big global challenges have lived in separate silos, organized in conflicting formats across different UN agencies. Connecting the dots often meant months of painstaking manual work for data analysts before any real analysis could begin. 

To solve this challenge, the UN system is launching the UN System Data Commons — an open-source platform built on Data Commons by Google that unites global statistics into one interconnected resource known as an AI-ready knowledge graph. With support from Google.org, the project breaks down data silos and makes critical statistics universally accessible, helping everyone from researchers to leaders track global progress in real time.

The system also lets people explore through intuitive, natural-language search — making it easier for anyone, from a nonprofit program manager to a journalist to an international policy analyst, to ask questions in plain language and instantly receive relevant data and interactive visualizations.

Over the coming year, we’ll continue adding datasets from more UN entities, with a goal of including 80% of UN system statistical datasets by 2027.

Explore the data: data.un.org

And learn more: goo.gle/4dKzE0y

“I was sitting in my office in San Francisco looking out the window one day and I couldn't see more than 30 feet because [the air] was completely filled with smoke,” says Google Research scientist, Chris Van Arsdale. “And then I realized that it was actually kind of my problem to deal with it, because fires are both a symptom of climate change and a driver of climate change. In the last six years that I've had my daughter, I really want to work on things that'll make the world better for her.”

Chris leads Google’s climate and energy research group, the team responsible for looking for ways we can use our technology to mitigate climate change. For over a decade, Google Research has been exploring how to use AI and machine learning to detect wildfires and model how fires spread.

We sat down with him in our latest Ask a Scientist installment to learn more about FireSat, a satellite designed to detect and monitor wildfires.

Ask Nitesh what he does at Google, and he'll tell you about the supply chain that outgrew its own systems, and how his team finally fixed it.

As a Staff Program Manager on our Global Infrastructure team, Nitesh led an initiative called the AlphaNet Supply Chain (ANI-SC) to unify how Google orders and delivers the materials that build its network. The work replaced years of disconnected systems and manual steps with automation, helping Google keep pace with 10 times the growth while giving on-site teams far more visibility into what's happening.

"What makes working at Google truly rewarding is the opportunity to tackle unprecedented, highly complex challenges alongside exceptionally talented colleagues who inspire you to excel every day," Nitesh says.

Explore opportunities to help build Google Cloud's infrastructure at scale → https://goo.gle/46yYsVD

We’re focusing this work in key areas where it matters most: making disease detectable, treatable, and preventable; predicting natural disasters; expanding learning; and unlocking economic opportunities for more people.

resharedPostContent.text:
Recently, I had the chance to sit down with Astronaut Christina Koch for one of the most fascinating and inspiring conversations I’ve had in years. 

Christina is a NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration astronaut, scientist, engineer, explorer, and, as I’m sure many of you know, a member of the Artemis II crew that recently went farther in space – beyond the moon –  than any humans have gone before. 

Among the many things that will stay with me from our dialogue is how she has returned many times to a fundamental question at the frontiers of science and discovery: “Do we go there and learn it, or do we declare it unknowable?”

That spirit framed our entire dialogue. Beyond her record-breaking achievements and the technical milestones during her time on the International Space Station and Artemis II mission – and the teamwork that made it all possible -- we discussed exploration, science, and the future partnership between astronauts, robotics, and AI. 

We also touched on the profound questions that define human exploration and discovery: What its like seeing Earth from above, whether its North Carolina or Ghana? What does seeing Earth as a “lifeboat” teach us about our own humanity? Why is cooperation, rather than raw intelligence alone, the key to an enduring civilization? What pushes us to advance the frontiers of exploration, science and discovery? And ultimately, what drives our search to know if we are alone in the universe?

Christina has already achieved so much, including many firsts, and I was curious about what advice she’d share with young people (grownups too) who aspire to future discovery and exploration. She had a number of helpful things to say – the one that stuck with me the most was: "if your dreams are only about yourself, you’re not dreaming big enough."

I hope you all enjoy this Dialogue as much as I did. You can watch it here: https://lnkd.in/eFd4NvAF

Last month, Grow with Google took our “Make AI Work for You” tour on the road, traveling Route 66 to bring hands-on AI training to small business owners across five states, teaching them ways to save time, boost sales, and grow their teams’ skills.

We partnered with local chambers of commerce and Small Business Development Centers across Missouri, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona, and California. Together, we showed local business owners how Gemini and Google Workspace can handle routine admin, draft marketing content, and win back hours in their day. 

Since its founding in 2017, Grow with Google has helped more than 13 million Americans learn digital skills to grow their careers and businesses. Now, with AI changing how we work, the impact of these skills is more vital than ever. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce reported that 85% of small businesses using AI saw an increase in sales last year, and 82% grew their teams. When local businesses thrive, the community benefits. 

Missed our Grow with Google tour along Route 66? U.S. small businesses and entrepreneurs can still get courses and resources at no cost at Grow.Google/SMB.

Learn more about our tour along Route 66 → https://goo.gle/4xeeQ8C
